Longbow. A medieval weapon, a tall simple bow made of yew wood standing nearly as tall as a man and capable of firing arrows with devastating force and speed. Developed and perfected by Welsh and English archers, the longbow proved devastatingly effective against armored knights during the Hundred Years' War, particularly at Crécy in thirteen forty-six and Agincourt in fourteen fifteen.

The weapon required years of training and conditioning to master. English law mandated practice for all able-bodied men to maintain a trained force of archers. It could fire arrows at a rate of six to ten per minute when used in massed formations, creating devastating volleys before close combat even began.

Arrows could penetrate armor and pierce knights from two hundred yards away, destroying the medieval myth of cavalry invincibility. At the Battle of Crécy in thirteen forty-six, English and Welsh archers decimated French cavalry charges, helping establish English dominance in the early Hundred Years' War. At Agincourt in fourteen fifteen, Henry the Fifth's archers again proved decisive, killing thousands of French knights and infantry in a mud-soaked valley where their advantage was maximized.

The longbow eventually became obsolete as firearms and pike-and-shot formations emerged in the sixteenth century, but its tactical innovations influenced military thinking for centuries.

It connects to the Battle of Crécy where longbows first decisively defeated French cavalry and changed medieval warfare, to the Battle of Agincourt where English archers achieved another famous victory, and to the Hundred Years' War in which English archers achieved their greatest fame and demonstrated superior tactics over mounted nobility.
